turn_text: Thanks, Megan. Crude oil prices remain relatively healthy, and despite ongoing COVID hotspots around the world, energy markets are banking on global oil demand, really rebounding in the back half of the year. But within the U.S., there remains the potential for key supply disruptions starting in May. The focus is on a handful of pipeline projects facing potential shutdowns from ongoing legal battles. Previously, President Biden effectively canceled the infamous Keystone XL Project in January. Next up, a federal judge is expected to rule in May whether to shutter the four-year-old Dakota Access Pipeline that is essentially operating illegally without a necessary water crossing easement. The judge is giving the U.S. Army Corps of Engineers one last chance to weigh in today on May 3rd And then he is going to decide whether to order the 570,000 barrel per day, buck and shale or artery shut. Any closure likely would last until spring 2022 when the Army Corps complete a more stringent environmental review to award the pipeline the needed easement. While Enbridge is just a minority owner of Dakota Access, the other fights are over Enbridge operated pipelines. The state of Michigan ordered the line five crude oil and propane system closed by May 12th for alleged safety risks. Court-ordered mediation talks are ongoing now, and while it is unlikely the 540,000 barrel per day pipeline closes in May, something is going to have to give within the coming days. Then there's Enbridge's Line 3 replacement pipeline system to move heavy Canadian crew to the US. The Enbridge project is more than 50% built, primarily in Minnesota, but a ruling on a long-shot legal bid to cease the work is expected to in May or June. Construction is currently on a spring break pause until the beginning of June, but Enbridge plans to bring the new pipeline into service by the end of this year. So in the coming days and weeks, energy markets are closely watching the U.S. court system. This has been Jordan Bloom with the Market Minute.
